entry.title: One person. An entire car.
entry.question: How much vehicle does it take to move one person?
entry.answer: Sharing a vehicle spreads its space and mass across more people. Sixty solo drivers need sixty cars; four per car need fifteen.
entry.explanation: An interactive essay separating vehicle occupancy, street capacity, fuel-energy conversion, moving vehicle mass and the case for compact communities with useful public transit.
entry.qualification: Vehicle counts are an illustrative model, not measured road area or real-world occupancy. Capacity ranges describe peak conditions; energy estimates describe specified test cycles. Mass per person is not energy efficiency or a lifecycle footprint. The mass-and-speed model calculates kinetic energy and an ideal equivalent drop height, not collision force, stopping distance or injury risk.
entry.whyCare: A street can be full of vehicles while doing surprisingly little to move people.

evidence.scope: Illustrative group of 60 travelers with 1, 2 or 4 people per car, including drivers; one bus with 60 passengers, excluding its driver. Global Street Design Guide capacity ranges for a 3-m lane or equivalent width under peak conditions with normal operations. U.S. DOE/EPA test-cycle energy estimates. Illustrative 4,000 lb car, excluding occupants. Separate traffic state: 32 solo drivers plus 60 bus passengers (92 travelers), with one additional bus operator. Original illustrative dense neighborhood model; qualitative land-use and transit relationships from EPA guidance. Original kinetic-energy thought experiment: illustrative vehicle weights 2,000–8,000 lb and speeds 10–60 mph. Equivalent ideal free fall, not actual crash outcomes. Direct trip-energy illustration: gasoline energy for a 30 US mpg car with 1–4 people versus gross metabolism of a 70 kg adult cycling at 11 mph (6.8 MET). No upstream energy, emissions or extra-food estimate.
evidence.dataAsOf: 2016 street design guide, reproduced in 2018 presentation; DOE EV summary September 16, 2024; undated DOE/EPA gasoline page; original illustrative model October 2026; EPA smart-growth guidance updated April 30, 2026; classical mechanics from OpenStax College Physics 2e; NHTSA speed-management synthesis checked October 2026; 2024 Adult Compendium cycling category 01020; DOE December 16, 2024 energy conversion; original October 6, 2026 trip model
evidence.denominator: People per vehicle; people per hour in a 3-m lane or equivalent width; percent of fuel energy in the gasoline vehicle; lb of illustrative vehicle per occupant. These denominators are not interchangeable. Kinetic energy displayed in foot-pounds and equivalent vertical free-fall height in feet, using specified total moving mass and speed. Direct energy input in Wh per person-mile or person-km. Fuel energy versus gross rider metabolism; excludes car occupants’ metabolism.
evidence.methodology: Vehicle counts: 60/n for n=1,2,4; bus illustration assumes 60 passengers. Mass allocation: 4000/n lb for n=1,2,3,4 (rounded only for display). Capacity ranges copied as factual values from Prati 2018 slide 23 (PDF page 23), with 3-m scope supplied by the Global Street Design Guide. Gasoline 18–25% energy to wheels in combined 55% city/45% highway test cycle. EV 87–91% includes net regenerative recovery; excludes lifecycle and electricity generation. No claim that 96% of energy is wasted moving vehicle mass. No causal congestion or citywide emissions estimate. Traffic scene: 32 solo cars + one bus carrying 60 passengers = 33 vehicles and 92 travelers; bus operator additional. This is a separate population from the fixed-60 comparison. Neighborhood camera views are conceptual design illustrations with no modeled travel time, capacity, density, energy or emissions output. K = 0.5*m*(mph*0.44704)^2 joules; ideal equivalent height h = (mph*0.44704)^2/(2*9.81) metres and fall time t = (mph*0.44704)/9.81 seconds. Weight in lb converted to kg with 0.45359237; energy J converted to foot-pounds by dividing by 1.3558179483314004; height m converted to feet by dividing by 0.3048. Display energy to whole foot-pounds and height to one decimal; unrounded calculations. Defaults 4000 lb and 30 mph; ranges 2000–8000 lb and 10–60 mph; fixed vertical scale 0–140 ft. Primary readout rounds height to whole feet and describes approximate stories at an explicitly illustrative 10 feet per story; actual building floors vary. A geometric building reference highlights the equivalent height. US tons = lb/2000. Foot-pound energy values remain in optional calculation details, not the primary readout. Reference energy uses the same mass at 20 mph. Doubling mass doubles energy; doubling speed quadruples energy and height. Free-fall height and time are independent of mass. Neglects air resistance and rotational energy; no impact-force, stopping-distance, casualty or injury prediction. Real collision harm depends on impact speed, vehicle shape and collision circumstances. Trip comparison: car Wh/person-mile = 33700 / US mpg / occupants; bike kcal/mile = 6.8*70/11, Wh/mile = kcal/mile*4184/3600; divide either by 1.609344 for Wh/person-km. Baseline 1123.333333 and 50.292525 Wh/person-mile, ratio 22.335990. Car range 15–60 US mpg (235.214583/mpg L/100 km), occupants 1–4; fuel held fixed with occupancy. Gross bike metabolism includes rest, not extra food consumed; excludes car occupants’ metabolism. No upstream food/fuel production, manufacturing, infrastructure or emissions. Compendium adult range 19–59; standardized estimate, not individual calorie prediction. Unit display uses kg, km/h, meters, tonnes and kJ without changing canonical mass/speed, drop geometry, animation timing or ratio.

fragment:
One person.
An entire car.

A seat for you. A machine around you. Now multiply that bargain by everyone trying to get somewhere.

Deep Dive · Space, energy & the cost of empty seats

Read the Deep Dive
SpaceEnergyCar vs. bikeMass & speedA better waySources

The people stay.
The cars don’t have to.

Put those same 60 people four to a car: 15 cars instead of 60. Give them a bus carrying 60 passengers: one passenger vehicle, with a driver too. The travelers have not vanished. The vehicles have.

A city’s job is to connect people to places. Counting how many cars get through tells only part of that story.

People per hour · 025,000
Private motor vehicles600–1,600
Two-way protected bikeway6,500–7,500
Dedicated transit lanes4,000–8,000
Sidewalk8,000–9,000
On-street transitway, bus or rail10,000–25,000

Each dark segment is a range, on the same zero-based scale. A lane about 10 feet wide (3 meters in the source), or equivalent width, at peak conditions with normal operations. These are design-guide capacities, not average ridership or a promise for every street. The private-vehicle range is not restricted to solo drivers. A two-way bikeway counts both directions. NACTO/GDCI, PDF p. 23; scope and assumptions.

A high-capacity transitway is a different facility from a bus sharing traffic. Stops, signals, service frequency, occupancy and safe access all matter. Space for walking and cycling also means space for trips that need no car at all.

So much energy.
So little motion.

For a conventional gasoline vehicle on the DOE/EPA combined city–highway cycle, about 18–25% of the fuel’s energy reaches the wheels. Most is lost in the engine, primarily as heat. And the wheels move the whole vehicle, along with whoever is inside.

Band widths show the 25%-to-wheels case; the remaining 75% is 100% minus 25%. Estimated combined cycle: 55% city, 45% highway. A range across vehicles, not a measurement of your trip. DOE/EPA: where the energy goes.

Electric cars change this part of the story. DOE reports 87–91% efficiency including energy recovered through regenerative braking. That vehicle-level figure does not include electricity generation or manufacturing. Electrifying a car still leaves a car to accommodate.

Occupancy changes the denominator. Energy per passenger-distance is vehicle energy divided by the people carried. A well-used bus can spread its energy use over many riders; a nearly empty one may not. Vehicle technology, route and occupancy decide the comparison. DOE’s EV explanation.

One person.
A much smaller appetite.

For the same distance, how much energy goes in? Here’s an illustrative gasoline car beside a conventional bicycle, measured per person carried.

Fuel energy for the car. The rider’s estimated total metabolic energy for the bike. Both expressed in watt-hours.

Units
15 US mpg60 US mpg

Move right for a more efficient car.

1 person4 people

Includes the driver. Fuel use is held fixed as occupancy changes.

Bike held fixed: 154 lb rider at 11 mph, using the 2024 Compendium’s 6.8-MET cycling category. About 43.3 dietary Calories per mile.

A model, not a measured trip or an individual calorie prediction. The bike value includes resting metabolism while riding; the car value excludes occupants’ metabolism. Neither includes producing the food or gasoline, building the vehicles or roads, or any emissions estimate. Wind, hills, riding style, the rider and driving conditions change the result. This is not a measure of energy reaching the wheels.

The assumptions and calculations

The baseline car gets an assumed 30 miles per US gallon (7.84 L/100 km) with one person aboard. Using DOE/EPA’s 33.7 kWh per US gallon: 33,700 ÷ 30 = 1,123.3 Wh per vehicle-mile. Divide by occupancy for energy per person-mile.

The bike model uses a 70 kg adult at an assumed 11 mph (17.702784 km/h), within Compendium activity 01020’s 10–11.9 mph category, rated at 6.8 METs. Using 1 MET ≈ 1 kcal/kg/hour: 6.8 × 70 ÷ 11 = 43.27 kcal/mile. With 1 kcal = 4,184 joules and 1 Wh = 3,600 joules, that is 50.29 Wh/mile. This is gross metabolism, not a prediction of extra food eaten. The Compendium is standardized for adults aged 19–59 and does not predict an individual’s precise expenditure.

Divide both per-mile values by 1.609344 for per-kilometer values: 698.01 Wh for the solo car and 31.25 Wh for the bike. Their ratio is about 22.34 before display rounding. Both bars begin at zero and use the same fixed scale. Changing units does not change their lengths or ratio.

Baseline model · one person in each mode
Direct energy inputWh/person-mileWh/person-km
Gasoline car · 30 US mpg1,123.33698.01
Bicycle · 70 kg, 11 mph50.2931.25

Download the baseline calculation (CSV)

Sources checked October 6, 2026: 2024 Compendium: cycling category 01020; MET definition and reuse terms; limits of individual estimates; DOE/EPA energy equivalence; NIST: calories and joules.

Heavy metal.
Fragile people.

A moving car carries energy that has to go somewhere when it stops. A vehicle twice as heavy carries twice the energy at the same speed. Double the speed and that energy quadruples. People outside the vehicle do not have a steel cabin around them.

Units
2,000 lb8,000 lb
10 mph60 mph
Try doubling it
Like dropping this car from30 feet.

Roughly 3 stories high.

That’s 2 US tons falling. More weight means more energy at the same height.

How the comparison works

The selected vehicle carries 120,345 foot-pounds of kinetic energy—2.25 times its energy at 20 mph. An ideal fall of 30.1 feet gives the same mass the same energy.

For the visual height reference, each story is 10 feet. Actual floor heights vary. Vehicle weight is illustrative, not a fleet average.

The energy is real.
The harm is not inevitable.

In a collision, energy can go into deformation, movement and heat. What happens to a person also depends on impact speed, vehicle shape, contact and how the collision unfolds. An energy calculation cannot predict someone’s injuries.

NHTSA links higher speeds and larger vehicles to greater dangers in crashes. Lower speeds, safer vehicles and streets designed around people matter alongside better alternatives to driving.

And before it moves,
it has to be made.

A vehicle also represents materials and manufacturing. Sharing an existing car uses the same machine for more travelers; it does not erase its production footprint. Replacing solo trips with fewer vehicles creates an opportunity to need fewer machines and less space to store them. Actual savings depend on what is built, how long it lasts and whether shared travel replaces ownership and driving.

Energy = ½ × mass × speed². Equivalent drop height = speed² ÷ (2 × gravity), using gravity ≈ 32.2 ft/s². Switch units to see kilograms, km/h, meters and kilojoules; the underlying scenario stays the same. OpenStax: kinetic energy · Gravitational energy. These are idealized calculations, not a stopping-distance, collision-force or injury model.

Bring life
closer.

More homes near the places we need.
Public transit that makes the connection.
A neighborhood built around living.

Put more life
within reach.

Allow more homes near shops, services and transit. Mix uses. Connect the blocks. Compact, mixed-use neighborhoods make walking, cycling and transit more convenient. Density can look like the apartments above a grocer, the rowhomes around a corner, the everyday places along a bus route.

Make transit
worth choosing.

A painted lane is only a start. The proposal here pairs dedicated bus space with frequent, reliable service, accessible stops and safe crossings. Build the neighborhood and fund the service together. EPA: connecting land use and transportation.

The goal is a place
you can live in.

Make room for more neighbors, different housing needs, and the people already there. Keep access for disabled people, deliveries and trips that still need a car. Give people a real alternative for the trips that do not.

A home near daily life.
A bus worth waiting for.
A street worth walking down.

Inspired by Bill Nye’s Human Transportation. The next step is a question of design: how do we make it easier to get where life happens?

The sources, the assumptions, the numbers

Different questions, different measures. The opening counts vehicles. The lane chart compares people per hour. The energy graphic compares fuel energy reaching the wheels. The mass-and-speed demonstration calculates translational kinetic energy and an equivalent ideal free-fall height. The source table separately allocates illustrative vehicle mass per occupant. None is a complete environmental score.

Illustrative group of 60 travelers
OccupancyVehiclesVehicle lb/personVehicle kg/person
1 per car604,0001,814.37
2 per car302,000907.18
3 per car201,333.33604.79
4 per car151,000453.59
60 bus passengers1 busNot modeledNot modeled

Car calculations: 60 ÷ occupants; 4,000 lb (1,814.36948 kg) ÷ occupants. Mass allocations in the table are rounded to two decimals. The mass-and-speed controls instead use kinetic energy = ½mv², with mph × 0.44704 to convert to m/s; equivalent free-fall height = v²/(2 × 9.81). Pounds are converted to kilograms with lb × 0.45359237; joules to foot-pounds with J ÷ 1.3558179483314004; meters to feet with m ÷ 0.3048. US mode displays whole foot-pounds and metric mode displays kilojoules to one decimal; detailed height is shown to one decimal in either feet or meters; calculations use unrounded values. A 4,000 lb vehicle at 20 mph carries 53,487 foot-pounds, at 40 mph 213,947 foot-pounds: exactly four times the energy before display rounding. Ideal drop time = v/9.81. These calculations omit wheel rotation and air resistance, and predict neither collision force nor injury. The bus adds an operator; it does not claim every bus has this capacity or occupancy. Vehicle silhouettes are schematic, with no distance, area or traffic-gap scale.

Design-guide capacity · people/hour per roughly 10-foot lane or equivalent width (3 m in source)
Mode/facilityRange
Private motor vehicles600–1,600
Two-way protected bikeway6,500–7,500
Dedicated transit lanes4,000–8,000
Sidewalk8,000–9,000
On-street transitway, bus or rail10,000–25,000

Ranges are planning guidance from the 2016 Global Street Design Guide, reproduced in Fabrizio Prati’s 2018 NACTO/GDCI presentation, PDF page 23. They are not measured 2026 flows or confidence intervals. Facility types and directions differ as labeled; the two-way bikeway includes both directions. No minimum/maximum ratio is presented as a guaranteed improvement.

Gasoline: DOE/EPA’s combined-cycle diagram estimates 18–25% to the wheels; the page’s broader 12–30% headline spans different drive cycles. EV: DOE’s September 16, 2024 summary reports 65–69% to wheels plus about 22% net regenerative recovery, yielding 87–91%. Do not multiply a passenger’s fraction of vehicle mass by either efficiency figure: drag, rolling resistance and other loads make that an invalid allocation of useful energy.
